title: BROINOWSKI, Gracius J. THE BIRDS OF AUSTRALIA: with a descriptive account of the life and characteristic habits of over seven hundred species.
description: BROINOWSKI, Gracius J. THE BIRDS OF AUSTRALIA: with a descriptive account of the life and characteristic habits of over seven hundred species. Six volumes in three, folio, with 303 full-page chromolithographs, contemporary half morocco, several tissue-guards or plates foxed, overall a very good set. Melbourne, Charles Stuart, 1887 – 1890 – 1891. Broinowski’s best-known work was designed to bring Australian ornithology to a much wider audience than could be reached by Gould’s expensive series of handcoloured lithographs published thirty years earlier. His production of over three hundred chromolithographs in Australia in 1890 was an exceptional undertaking and his book a monument to Australian printing technology and to the author’s remarkable enthusiasm. title: CARNEGIE, Honourable David W. SPINIFEX AND SAND: A Narrative of Five Years’ Pioneering and Exploration in Western Australia.
description: CARNEGIE, Honourable David W. SPINIFEX AND SAND: A Narrative of Five Years’ Pioneering and Exploration in Western Australia. Octavo, with half-title, two folding maps in the text (short tears), and two folding maps loose in a back endpocket, a frontispiece portrait and 44 other illustrations (some full-page) are included in the pagination; in lightly marked original primary fawn cloth, the spine lettered and decorated in gilt, the front board lettered and illustrated in black, top edge gilt, others uncut; a very good copy of a book usually found otherwise. London, C. Arthur Pearson Limited, 1898. First edition – and a much superior copy – of one of the most enthralling works of inland exploration. An enthusiastic prospector on the Western Australian goldfields, Carnegie led his first, ninety-day, expedition in 1894 in which he covered approximately 850 miles of largely unexplored territory around Hampton Plains, Victoria Springs, Mount Shenton, and Mount Ida. His subsequent 1896-7 expedition was to establish the nature of the country between the southern goldfields and the Kimberleys in the north, and between the east-west routes taken by Warburton and Forrest in 1874. On this expedition, which lasted eight months and covered 3000 miles, Carnegie crossed and explored the vast unexplored deserts of the interior, facing a daily battle of survival with little food and less water. Carnegie and his men fought off death many times and endured quite exceptional hardship. For his outstanding work in one of Australia’s most inhospitable wildernesses Carnegie was awarded the Gill Memorial medal of the Royal Geographical Society. “One of the most enthralling works of inland exploration. As a writer, Carnegie is without rival in the entire literature of Australian inland exploration” (Wantrup). Ferguson, 7960; Wantrup, 196a. Provenance: W.H.S. Osmond with armorial bookplate. Dr. F. title: GRANT, James. THE NARRATIVE OF A VOYAGE OF DISCOVERY, performed in His Majesty’s Vessel The Lady Nelson, of sixty tons b
description: GRANT, James. Quarto, with large folding plate of sliding keels and a folding chart (both laid down on fine linen at the time of binding), six plates (one handcoloured), with the rare blank leaf d4 but without the leaf of subscribers that sometimes replaces it, the fore-edge of the title a little dusted, bound with generous margins in early twentieth-century half morocco, top edge gilt, J. Walter Tyas bookplate. London, Printed by C. Rowarth for T. Egerton, 1803 First edition of one of the foundation works for Victoria, recording the discovery of the Victorian coast. In 1800 James Grant was instructed to sail the Lady Nelson from England to Sydney where it was intended he would hand her over to Matthew Flinders. In the course of the voyage, Grant was instructed to search for the western passage into Bass Strait and traverse it from west to east. This he succeeded in doing, discovering the Victorian coastline west of Bass’s discoveries of 1797 and 1798. Subsequently, in 1801, Grant and Lieutenant-Governor William Paterson, explored the Hunter River in the Lady Nelson. As a result of Paterson’s report Governor King established the future city of Newcastle. Shortly after this trip Grant returned to England and command of the Lady Nelson passed to Lieutenant John Murray. Grant published this substantial voyage account upon his return to England. This handsome work is well illustrated with a large folding plate of sliding keels, a folding chart of Bass Strait, a finely handcoloured plate of the Fringe Crested Cockatoo, and five engraved plates. title: GREY, George. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS OF DISCOVERY IN NORTH-WEST AND WESTERN AUSTRALIA, during the years 1837, 38, a
description: GREY, George. JOURNALS OF TWO EXPEDITIONS OF DISCOVERY IN NORTH-WEST AND WESTERN AUSTRALIA, during the years 1837, 38, and 39, Under the Authority of Her Majesty’s Government. Describing many newly discovered, important, and fertile Districts, with Observations on the moral and physical Condition of the Aboriginal Inhabitants, &c. &c. By George Grey, Esq. Governor of South Australia; Late Captain of the Eighty-third Regiment. Two volumes, octavo, with two large folding maps loose in an endpocket in volume one, with 22 plates (six coloured), advertisement leaf in volume one, with early owner’s signature of G. Hance on both titles; entirely uncut in the original primary dark violet cloth, the spines very lightly faded, an uncommonly fine and bright copy. London, T. & W. Boone, 1841. One of the finest copies we have seen, perhaps rivalling even the Phillipps copy (which was in the same variant binding). First edition of a classic Western Australian exploration account. In July 1837 Grey sailed for Australia on board the Beagle to explore the land in Australia’s north-west with a view to establishing a permanent settlement there. In the course of his two expeditions, both of which were undertaken in extreme hardship, Grey discovered and named the Glenelg River, the Macdonald Range, the Stephen Range, the Gairdner River, Mount Lyell, the Gascoyne River, the Murchison River and nine other rivers, the Lyell, Victoria and Gairdner Ranges, and many other features along the west coast. Grey’s expeditions and the associated coastal surveys of Wickham and Stokes in the Beagle, were a major advance in the discovery of the west and north-west parts of the Australian continent. Grey’s narrative includes scientific appendices by John Gould, John Edward Gray, and Adam White. The Aboriginal rock paintings found on the first expedition are illustrated on several plates. The officially sanctioned account of the new colony, it is a full record of events both on land and on sea in the first months of the settlement from March 1787, just before the First Fleet sailed, up to September 1788. The text records the early expeditions of Phillip and the other officers into the interior around Botany Bay and Port Jackson, and the earliest coastal voyages of discovery. Text and plates illustrate newly discovered animal life, and among the charts and plans (most notably by John Hunter and William Dawes) is the earliest plan of the settlement at Sydney Cove, showing what buildings and other progress had been made there by July 1788. Finally, although far from complete, an appendix lists the convicts embarked on the First Fleet. title: WALKER, C.B. PHOTOGRAPHS MELBOURNE & SUBURBS by C.B. Walker [cover title].
description: WALKER, C.B. PHOTOGRAPHS MELBOURNE & SUBURBS by C.B. Walker [cover title]. 35 albumen paper photographic prints, mounted as issued in original photographer’s studio album, oblong octavo, original black half, pebble-grain black cloth sides, front board title in gilt, pale tide mark on lower board Melbourne, circa 1890s. Attractive and rare photographic album from the land boom era of ‘Marvellous Melbourne’. Little was known of photographer Charles Bristow Walker’s before the Miegunyah Press publication reproducing an album in the Baillieu Library, University of Melbourne. Ian Morrison edited that publication and has since updated the information on Walker and his album in an article in the journal of the Bibliographical Society of Australia and New Zealand (Script & Print, Vol. 29 (2005), pp. 234-246). It is evident that Walker published the album not as a collection of photographs but more as a ‘binder’ that could be made up as the purchaser wished with either thirty or sixty photographs, or presumbly anywhere in between. Examples of the published albums are known in either form. The combination of images in the few known copies of the album vary the one from the others, which reflect the original owner’s taste and interests. That the physical album was issued more as a binder than a suite of images is supported, for example, by three copies of the album sold by us, one of which had fifty-eight views, six of which were of Sydney, another album of only twenty-two Melbourne views but probably with some (eight?) removed, and the Aitken copy with thirty Melbourne views. The nature of the album as a binder also explains the otherwise slightly puzzling fact that in the known albums, the identifying captions are in manuscript rather than printed. Nine of the thirty-five photos in the current album share a title with ones in Morrison’s book, but all are different (in small or large ways). Provenance: inscribed from architect Sam Brittingham in 1889. Samuel Charles Brittingham was chief architect of the Victorian public works department and was associated with the design of the Old Arts Building (University of Melbourne), the Parkville Post Office, and the Mount Buffalo Chalet. Estimate $4000/6000 Illustrated online at www.invaluable .com

title: BEAN, C.E.W. (editor).
description: BEAN, C.E.W. (editor). It is rarely, if ever, spelt out but the misattribution on page 104 is due to an Anzac submitting, one hopes waggishly, a poem by Arthur Adames as his own. The Anzac Book is of one of the most significant literary productions of the war and arguably one of the key books of the first century of the Commonwealth. This book was produced in the lines at Anzac Cove on Gallipoli in 1915. Virtually every contribution (Adams apart) was written or drawn in the trenches under fire. The Anzac Book, is a monument to the men of Anzac and their spirit, expressed both through their creative efforts and through the official mythographic narrative of their deeds of war. title: KNIGHT, William Thomas.
description: KNIGHT, William Thomas. COLLINS STREET IN 1844. Lithographed leaf, 230 x 170 mm, on thick card removed from a late C19th Australian stock album, signed in the image bottom left “F.H.”; unrelated contemporary portrait photograph mounted on verso. This was the earliest known published view of the new city. W.T. Knight’s sketch of Melbourne from an elevated position on Collins Street looking west, was made on a business trip there from Van Diemen’s Land in mid-1839. His rather primitive topographic sketch, with figures of settlers, animals, and a group of Aborigines in the foreground was then lithographed by Edward Noyce for prominent London map and print publisher Joseph Cross, who published the view in August 1840 as “Collins Street – Town of Melbourne, Port Philip, New South Wales” (310 x 285 mm). A number of late 19th century variants are known and there is a watercolour version of the Cross lithograph in the National Library. An albumen paper photograph print from circa 1860 by John Hunter Kerr appears to be of Knight’s now lost sketch. The view along Collins Street, from near Russell Street looking west towards Market Street, shows the entire township of about thirty or forty buildings, three sailing ships at dock to the distant left of Collins Street, a vegetable garden and its picket fence lower right, and a group of Aboriginal people surveying the scene from the high ground in the foreground of the image. The lithographer of the present piece title, ‘F.H.’, presumably worked from the Noyce-Cross lithograph, although the error of date in the title, ‘1844’ for ‘1840’, is curious given that the original lithograph is clearly dated 1840. Knight’s sketch is now lost, as mentioned above, although an album in the Joachim Collection (Australian Book Auctions and Mossgreen Auctions, June 2016, lot 526) of his own 1861 photographs of Melbourne included a photograph of Knight’s 1839 sketch. The present lithograph by ‘F.H.’ has small variations from the Noyce-Cross lithograph and in some respects is perhaps slightly closer to Knight’s original sketch, which suggests that the present version may have been taken from Kerr’s photograph or, possibly, even Wright’s original sketch. Estimate $200/400 Illustrated online at www.invaluable .com Lot 88
